https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-tarif.text: LIVERPOOL, England — Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds is keeping tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles “under review” as the U.K. fights to be included in Brussels’ Buy European program. The European Union has requested that the U.K. raise tariffs on Chinese EVs in order to advance talks to join the industrial program, amid fears Britain could provide a back door for Chinese vehicles to enter the single market, the Financial Times reported on Friday . During an interview at The POLITICO Pub at Labour Party conference, Reynolds said he is keeping the issue of tariffs on Chinese EVs “under review, to be frank, more closely than lots of other issues” and that “different parts of our own sector want different things from” the government’s policy. Advertisement Advertisement EU capitals are currently considering whether U.K. auto exports should qualify for preferential treatment under the Buy European program, as Brussels moves to protect its member economies from U.S. tariffs, China’s manufacturing might and an influx of cheap EVs subsidized by Beijing. European Union lawmakers and officials are preparing new legislation to deny overseas manufacturers access to subsidies, tax incentives and public procurement deals. The bloc slapped double-digit tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. But Reynolds said the U.K. government’s calculation on whether to impose tariffs differed from that of the EU. “We are an export-orientated sector. So clearly, you shouldn’t do anything that risks your export markets, and you always have to take heed of retaliatory action if you put tariffs in place,” he said Sunday, calling the U.K.’s position on Chinese EVs “finely balanced.” Cutting the U.K. out of Brussels’ new industrial program “wouldn’t be to the benefit of Europe,” Reynolds added. The Made in Europe push is supposed to be “about greater resilience, greater autonomy for European industry in the face of very significant pressures from both the U.S. and China,” Reynolds added. “Now, if that is the objective, it stands to reason that the U.K., that’s the second-biggest economy in Europe, should be a part of that.” Advertisement Advertisement Non-U.K. goods moving from Britain to the EU must pay applicable tariffs. But Reynolds has said he’s open to Chinese EV-makers setting up in Britain. Chinese firms have been eyeing Britain as a home base, with Nissan striking an MoU for Chinese EV giant Chery to use one of its Sunderland factory lines to make EVs in June. Excluding U.K. supply chains from Made in Europe could cost €24 billion in economic activity on the EU side alone, the British SMMT automotive lobby warned earlier this month. Britain’s chemical and energy supply chains could also face restrictions under the rules. The tussle between London and Brussels over the degree to which the U.K. should be included in European supply chains threatens to delay a major summit to wrap up talks on a range of trade issues later this year. Reynolds also warned that “constitutional questions” regarding Britain’s EU relationship are causing “uncertainty” for business. The senior Cabinet minister said the U.K. should be focused on “how we can improve that trade relationship,” rather than whether Labour should push for Britain to rejoin the bloc.

https://www.politico.eu/article/17-count.text: BRUSSELS — Seventeen EU governments have publicly warned against cuts to agriculture and regional payouts in the next seven-year budget , in a rebuke of Germany's stance in the negotiations. The letter — signed on Friday by Italy, Spain and Poland among others — heaps pressure on the Irish rotating presidency of the Council of the EU to leave untouched almost €900 billion of spending in the upcoming draft budget, which is expected to be presented next week. This sets up tensions with a rival camp of six countries led by Germany, which renewed calls for cuts of several hundred billion euros across the board in a joint letter earlier this week. Advertisement Advertisement "We therefore believe that the overall funding for Cohesion Policy and the CAP must be preserved in the next MFF," the seventeen countries wrote in the letter to Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin seen by POLITICO. The signatories include Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Romanian President Nicușor Dan coordinated the initiative and will host an informal meeting of those countries in the margins of the next European Council on Oct. 15 and 16. The Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF, finances everything from farmers’ subsidies to development aid, and is among the toughest negotiations in Brussels. In 2025, the European Commission proposed a budget of nearly €2 trillion for the 2028-2034 period and shifted hundreds of billions from agriculture and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, to new priorities such as defense and competitiveness. The so-called Friends of Cohesion group warned that further reductions to agricultural and cohesion "would only weaken it [budget] and risk undermining public support for the European project." Ireland’s negotiating document, or negobox, will set the scene for discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during the summit in Brussels in October. Advertisement Advertisement EU governments are rushing to secure a final agreement among themselves by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Poland and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations. One of the most sensitive issues involves introducing new EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, to finance the budget. The Commission proposed five new levies that are estimated to generate €66 billion per year. The tax package is strongly supported by France, but individual proposals have been opposed by several national governments who fear that they will be disproportionately affected by the levies. The 17 countries wrote in the letter that new own resources"should be genuine, fair, simple and non-regressive." To create more leeway, they also renewed calls to delay repayments of post-Covid debt that is expected to cost €25 billion per year and opposed budget discounts to wealthier countries, known as rebates.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones By Dan Sales Published 15 November 2026, 17:57 GMT Updated 2 hours ago A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. "We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said. The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks. Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment. US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says Published 23 hours ago Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace. The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump. Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back". It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented. The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher. On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there". "Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design. On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine. "It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying. Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets. Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said. It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions. Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions. Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said. Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram. Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk. "On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram. "Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack." Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said. In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said. Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company. Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems. The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented. "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
